children: The Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India's (IRDAI) proposed limits on management expenses and commissions will challenge the expansion of insurance businesses in Tier 3 and Tier 4 cities, Swami Saran Sharma, Founder and CEO at Helius Global Solutions, told CNBC-TV18.

A new 160-page consultation paper outlines five major changes for the sector: rationalising expenses of management, reintroducing segmental commissions, prohibiting dark patterns, mandating commission disclosures on policy documents, and streamlining motor insurance. Segmental commissions for motor and health insurance are being reintroduced because their removal in 2023 did not succeed in making policies cheaper.

Currently, the management expense limit is 30 percent for general insurance companies and 35 percent for standalone health insurance companies. Under the proposals, general and life insurance companies must achieve an expenses limit of 15 percent of the premium in two years and 12.5 percent in five years. A separate limit of 25 percent in two years and 20 percent in five years was also outlined for general insurance.

The regulator aims to prohibit distributors from seeking personal details such as phone numbers and email addresses before displaying product prices and features. This restriction will be a major point for players like PB Fintech, which generates 80 percent of its business through call centre assistance. Additionally, original equipment manufacturers (OEMs) selling motor insurance must inform policyholders that the same product is available on platforms like Bima Sugam at a commission of no more than 5 percent. For example, a policyholder buying a ₹100 product must be told it is available elsewhere for a ₹5 commission.

Assessing the regulatory shift, the Helius Global Solutions executive viewed the concept paper as an attempt to reintroduce rules removed in 2023, highlighting the regulator's dual responsibility of overseeing both regulation and business development. Expanding into smaller cities requires distribution channels that do not come cheap due to volume, making it difficult for personal lines of insurance to stay within the proposed limits. Business lines are less affected due to existing competition.
"When they press the pedal on development, regulations go for a toss and vice versa," Sharma noted, warning that squeezing commissions will affect overall business.

The draft rules also propose plugging alternative distributor payouts, such as foreign trips and gifts, under the new expense regulations. While the commission cuts may promote unhealthy competition, it remains unclear whether the resulting savings will ultimately benefit the consumer.
"This paper doesn't say anything about it because if the savings are affected, then I think it will do a lot good to the customer in case they are properly passed on," the CEO added.

Addressing the direct impact on distributors, the firm's founder supported rationalising payouts for mandated "pull products" like motor insurance, where the effort to secure a policy is very low. However, the same approach will not work for low-premium segments such as liability insurance, where the required effort is not commensurate with lower commissions.

title: IRDAI commission caps will challenge insurance expansion in smaller cities, says Helius Global CEO
